1	# Where it could go further
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A critic has already written a crit of a design. Your one job is to write the section "Where it could go further": what a stronger version of this piece would commit to, beyond fixing what the crit found. You do not change the crit, edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the image whole. When your prompt names several images, they are one page at several viewports, not versions: read each one, and build on the page as a whole. Look closely at anything you build an idea on. If the image is taller than one screen, you may run `node scripts/crop.mjs <in.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops it prints, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run it as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
12	2. Read the crit file. Note what it says the piece is for, every item under "What would move it most" with its number, and every item under "Smaller things".
13	3. Write the section by the rules below.
14	
15	## The rules
16	
17	- **Up to three numbered commitments** a stronger version of this piece would make. Fewer items are fine.
18	- **Each one starts from a specific element of this piece and names it.** Suggest that the piece own one color, let one number lead, or commit to one typeface only when that color, number, or typeface is already in the piece.
19	- **Each one names what the piece is for and how the commitment serves that.** Take the purpose from the crit's "What it's for".
20	- **Each one is marked taste and argues for itself.** Cite a source from the list in `agents/critic.md` under "Sources you may cite" when one states the idea, by author and work or by standard and number. Never invent a source or a figure.
21	- **Direction, not redesign.** Say what the commitment is and why, and leave the design to the designer.
22	- **Nothing repeated.** Before you write an item, check it against the ranked list and "Smaller things". When it grows out of a finding, start it with "Builds on finding N", where N is that finding's number in "What would move it most", and give only the new commitment. When nothing new is left, drop the item.
23	- **Nothing beyond the findings.** When the findings already say it all, write "Nothing beyond the findings." as the whole body of the section.
24	- **Never invent content.** Build each item only from what the piece already holds: never invent a fact, figure, name, comparison, quote, or sample for it, and never write new copy. When an idea needs content the piece does not have, name the kind of content and leave it to the maker.
25	- **Plain language.** Talk like a sharp designer across a table from a peer. No jargon you would not say aloud, no hedging. Write US spelling (color, center, gray, organize).
26	
27	## What you return
28	
29	Your final message is the section and nothing else: no preface, no other heading, no copy of the crit. It starts with the bold heading on its own line.
30	
31	```
32	**Where it could go further.**
33	1. <Commitment>: the element it starts from, what it commits to, how that serves what the piece is for, marked taste, with a source if one states it.
34	2. ...
35	```
36	
37	or, when nothing new is left:
38	
39	```
40	**Where it could go further.** Nothing beyond the findings.
41	```
42	
43	The caller puts the section into the crit after "What's working".
44

1	**First read.** On the desktop the eye goes first to the large serif headline, then across to the two dark green squares (plots 3 and 8) in the plot map, then down to the green "Add your garden" button. It reads as a calm, modest admin tool for someone who runs a garden: warm off-white, garden green, nothing loud. On the phone the first thing you see is a collision. The nav links sit on top of the "Plotwise" wordmark, the plot map runs off the right edge, and the four feature cards turn into narrow strips with one word per line.
2	
3	**What it's for.** A landing page that gets people who run community gardens to add their garden to Plotwise. It does this by showing that Plotwise replaces the spreadsheet they use now for plots and the waiting list (as you told me).
4	
5	**Verdict.** On desktop and tablet the page does its job. The headline names the tool the viewer already uses and promises to replace it, and there is one clear button. The biggest problem is the phone layout. At 390 px the page is 497 px wide, the header falls apart, and the feature text can't be read. After that, the plot map shows plot occupancy, not the waiting list the headline sells.
6	
7	**What would move it most**
8	
9	1. **The phone layout breaks.** The page is 497 px wide at a 390 px viewport, so it scrolls sideways (facts file `page_width`, phone). The plot map card starts at x 294 and runs off the right edge, and its left edge touches the last letter of "spreadsheet" in the headline. In the header, the four nav links wrap into three lines on top of the wordmark. "For growers" splits over two lines, which gives a 168×42 link box that sits over the logo. "For gardens" and "Pricing" are only 19 px tall and touch their neighbors, below the 24 px minimum (`violations`, target-size, `nav.site-nav > a:nth-of-type(1)` and `(3)`; WCAG 2.5.8). The four feature cards stay side by side, so their text runs 3.9 to 6.4 characters per line (`characters_per_line`, `div.cards > div.card > p`). The titles break inside the phrase ("Waiting / list", "Work / days"), so the viewer sees a column of single words, not a sentence. A garden committee member who opens a shared link on their phone sees a broken page before they read the offer. This is a defect (WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow; Bringhurst on measure, 45 to 75 characters). Fix direction: at phone width, stack everything in one column. Put the plot map below the button, put the cards one under another, and collapse the nav into a menu or put it on its own row. Viewports: phone
10	
11	2. **The plot map shows the wrong idea, and it can be read two ways.** The headline promises to run the waiting list and to offer a free plot to the next person in line. The picture next to it shows twelve plots with two highlighted, and nothing about a waiting list, a person, or an offer. So the picture backs up only "keeps the plots", the least distinct part of the claim. Also, the free plots are the dark, filled squares. On a plot map, a filled square easily reads as a plot that is taken or planted. The viewer has to find the small legend under the map to learn that it means the opposite. The title "Elm Row Gardens, plots 1 to 12" names what the map is, not what it shows. This is taste, argued on its own terms (no approved source covers how picture and headline pair). Labeling the free plots on the map itself, not through a legend, follows Tufte. Fix direction: make the picture show the step only Plotwise does, a free plot going to the next person on the waiting list. At least label plots 3 and 8 as free on the map and let the title state what the viewer should see. Use only states and names the product really has. Viewports: all
12	
13	3. **The section heading, card titles, and card text are all the same.** "What Plotwise does", "Waiting list", and "Growers join the list online…" are all 15 px, weight 400, #55604f (`font_size`, `font_weight`, `color` for `h2`, `div.card > h3`, `div.card > p`, every viewport). Also, no space separates a card title from its text. So each card reads as one sentence: "Waiting list Growers join the list online and see where they stand." A viewer who skims the cards, which is what cards are for, cannot pick out the four features. The section heading looks like a caption that floated away. This is a defect (Müller-Brockmann and Lupton: each level must be distinct at a glance). Fix direction: separate the card titles from their text by weight or color, not by a new size (Refactoring UI: bolder, not bigger). Add a small gap below each title. Viewports: all
14	
15	**Smaller things.**
16	- At widescreen the hero text stays 520 px wide on the left and the plot map sits against the right margin, with about 850 px of empty space between them. The cards stretch to 440 px wide with one line each, and the lower half of the screen is empty. Cap the content width so the hero reads as one unit. Viewports: widescreen
17	- The plot map card's left edge (x 797 on desktop) lines up with none of the feature card columns below it (x 646, 937). Place it on the card grid. Viewports: desktop, widescreen
18	- On the tablet the plot tiles shrink to 19 to 26 px wide, each a different width (`box`, `div.plot`). The card text runs 12 to 15 characters per line. Use two columns of cards and fixed tile widths. Viewports: tablet
19	- A single short word ends a paragraph: "yes." alone in the "Plot offers" card and "March." alone in "Rent reminders". Viewports: desktop, tablet, widescreen
20	- "Each grower gets one reminder before rent is due in March" and "who has a week to say yes" can be read as fixed limits of the product, or as one garden's settings. A garden with rent due in October may think Plotwise doesn't fit them. Make it clear whether these are examples or rules. Viewports: all
21	- "What Plotwise does" could be the heading on any product's page. It names a category, not what the section holds. Viewports: all
22	
23	**What's working.**
24	- The headline "Run the waiting list for your garden without the spreadsheet" sets the product against the tool the viewer already uses. That lets them judge the value on their own terms. Keep that comparison.
25	- There is one primary button, and its label names a concrete first step ("Add your garden"), not "Get started".
26	- The palette and type pairing (Source Serif 4 headline, Inter text, off-white and one garden green) fit a volunteer-run, outdoor audience. Every text color passes contrast at 5.33:1 or higher.
27	
28	**Couldn't judge from a still.**
29	- Whether the phone nav has a menu toggle that failed to render. Check in a live browser at 390 px.
30	
31	**Checklist.**
32	The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (image and headline make one idea)
33	What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (distinct levels below the first element)
34	Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 8 yes, 5 no (one grid; space inside groups smaller than between; no overlap; margin from page edge; empty space gathered)
35	Text: 30 lines, 26 yes, 4 no (line length; rag; widows; line breaks in headings)
36	Color: 9 lines, 9 yes
37	Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (logo clear space)
38	Charts and data: 16 lines, 14 yes, 2 no (direct labels; title states the finding)
39	Interface: 33 lines, 29 yes, 3 no (target size; platform conventions; reflow), 1 unsure (focus indicator)
40	Template tells: 10 lines, 10 yes

summary:
**Where it could go further.**
1. **Give the garden green one meaning.** On this page the green fills the "Add your garden" button and plots 3 and 8, and the legend labels it "Free." Commit to making green stand for one thing: an open place, either the free plot or the free spot for the visitor's own garden. Nothing else should be green. The visitor is a garden organizer, and a free plot is the moment they care about most. If the button and the free plot share one color that means "open," the page's one action points back to the product's one promise. Taste; Albers, *Interaction of Color*, shows that a color takes its meaning from how it is used around it, and this page is small enough to keep that use strict.
2. **Show the four cards as one plot's year, not four equal tiles.** "Waiting list," "Plot offers," "Rent reminders," and "Work days" already run in the order a plot moves through: someone joins the list, gets the plot, pays rent, and turns up to work. Commit to that order as a sequence the eye follows, not a row of equal features. A spreadsheet holds these as separate tabs. Plotwise's case is that it holds them as one flow, and a sequence makes that case without new copy. Taste, argued on its own terms.
3. **Builds on finding 2. Let Elm Row Gardens tie the page together.** The map already names one garden and two free plots. Once the map shows the offer, carry that same garden and those same plots into the cards, so every feature reads as something that happens to plot 3 or plot 8. The page needs no more than that one garden. The maker supplies the states and steps the product really has. One concrete case is easier to picture yourself in than four general claims, and that matters to an organizer who is judging whether Plotwise fits their own garden. Taste, argued on its own terms.

1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",

36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.

171:## Template tells
172-
173-Stock moves of AI-made templates that a viewer has seen on many other products, so the piece looks like anyone's. When a defect is the stock move one of these questions names, it belongs here rather than to a general question. A line about something the piece does not have is yes.
174-
175-[Omitted long context line]
176-- [ ] **Does the color scheme have a character of its own, rather than text in many tints of one hue, a highlight treatment on nearly every element so that none stands out, or a stock dark ground whose only color is one button?** → `references/tells.md` "Many near-identical tints of one hue for text"; `references/tells.md` "Every element highlighted"; `references/tells.md` "Neutral dark template look"
177-- [ ] **Is the type set without stock moves such as the heaviest weights on headings, small uppercase letterspaced labels, tightly tracked small text, or italic emphasis in interface text?** → `references/tells.md` "Headings at weight 800 or 900"; `references/tells.md` "Uppercase labels with wide tracking"; `references/tells.md` "Negative letter spacing on small text"; `references/tells.md` "Italic used for emphasis in interface text"
178-- [ ] **Does one screen keep to a small set of type sizes and weights, rather than a new size or weight for element after element, and are numbers of one kind in one format?** → `references/tells.md` "Too many type sizes and weights on one screen"; `references/tells.md` "Numbers in mixed formats"
179-- [ ] **Do the icons come from one set, in one size, color, and column, with no emoji or sparkle standing in for an icon or decoration?** → `references/tells.md` "Emoji as icons or status"; `references/tells.md` "Emoji inside pills and counts"; `references/tells.md` "Icons in many sizes and colors"; `references/tells.md` "Icons nudged off the column"; `references/tells.md` "Sparkle icon as decoration"
180-- [ ] **Are pills and badges kept for real status, few and without glow, rather than on every control, count, and feature?** → `references/tells.md` "Glowing pills for counts and status"; `references/tells.md` "PRO, New, and Beta badges everywhere"; `references/tells.md` "Every element a full pill"
181-- [ ] **Do the charts and stat cards look made for their data, rather than stock decoration such as rainbow or glowing bars, every series in shades of the accent, a sparkline on every card, or a row of identical chart cards?** → `references/tells.md` "Rainbow, glowing, or pill-shaped chart bars"; `references/tells.md` "Every chart in shades of the accent"; `references/tells.md` "Sparklines on every stat card"; `references/tells.md` "Equal cards side by side with the same chart"
182-- [ ] **Is the logo a mark of its own, rather than a stock gradient tile, sparkle, or glossy orb?** → `references/tells.md` "Gradient logo tile with a sparkle"; `references/tells.md` "Logo mark as a glossy orb"
183-- [ ] **Is the hero and the section after it laid out for this piece, rather than the stock template of a pill badge, a centered stack, a crowd of buttons, and a row of emoji feature cards?** → `references/tells.md` "Pill badge above the headline"; `references/tells.md` "Hero stacked on one centered axis"; `references/tells.md` "Three or more buttons in the hero"; `references/tells.md` "Feature cards with an emoji and a bold title"
184-[Omitted long context line]

=== references/tells.md
### Feature cards with an emoji and a bold title

- **Rule:** Feature cards use line icons or no icons, not one emoji per card above a bold title and one line of text.
- **Look for:** Is there a row of feature cards, each with an emoji, a bold title, and one line of text?
- **Source:** unslop by Damir Sokolovsky, CC BY 4.0, skills/unslop/references/signs.md, commit 620163eedb3529d9cd23a3994ed8d287d06f760d, group "Landing pages and heroes": "Feature cards with an emoji, a bold title and a vague line each → fewer features, concrete copy, line icons or none". Part of unslop by Damir Sokolovsky (@heydamir), CC BY 4.0. Changes: whether the line is vague and the call for concrete copy judge what the text says (NG-5, NG-10), so the entry keeps only the visual pattern.
- **Link:** https://github.com/heydamir/unslop/blob/620163eedb3529d9cd23a3994ed8d287d06f760d/skills/unslop/references/signs.md
=== references/tells.md
### Too many type sizes and weights on one screen

- **Rule:** One screen uses a few sizes from one scale and two weights, 400 and 500.
- **Look for:** Does one screen show six or more different text sizes, or three or more weights?
- **Source:** unslop by Damir Sokolovsky, CC BY 4.0, skills/unslop/references/signs.md, commit 620163eedb3529d9cd23a3994ed8d287d06f760d, group "Type": "Too many sizes and weights on one screen → a few sizes from the scale, weights 400 and 500". - **Link:** https://github.com/heydamir/unslop/blob/620163eedb3529d9cd23a3994ed8d287d06f760d/skills/unslop/references/signs.md

You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and no element the fix added or changed is a template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but an element the fix added or changed is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the fix added or changed as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. Added means the after image has it and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background. Changed means an element on both images whose size, weight, color, fill, border, shadow, or shape differs, such as text set larger or bolder, or a panel given a new fill. An added or changed element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and an element the fix added or changed is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40	
41	**What it's for.** One sentence, from the work order's crit or your stated assumption.
42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.
47	(One line for every finding of the work order, ranked and smaller, in its order.)
48	
49	**New problems.** One line each: where it is and what the viewer meets. Write "None." when there are none.
50	
51	**What would move it most**
52	1. <Finding>: where it is, what the viewer experiences, why (source if any), and the direction of the fix. Mark it defect, convention, or taste.
53	2. ...

55

57

59	```

1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.

1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and no element the fix added or changed is a template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but an element the fix added or changed is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the fix added or changed as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. Added means the after image has it and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background. Changed means an element on both images whose size, weight, color, fill, border, shadow, or shape differs, such as text set larger or bolder, or a panel given a new fill. An added or changed element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and an element the fix added or changed is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35

40

42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.
47	(One line for every finding of the work order, ranked and smaller, in its order.)
48	
49	**New problems.** One line each: where it is and what the viewer meets. Write "None." when there are none.
50	
51	**What would move it most**
52	1. <Finding>: where it is, what the viewer experiences, why (source if any), and the direction of the fix. Mark it defect, convention, or taste.
53	2. ...
54	(Write "None." under the heading when nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece.)
55	
56	**Smaller things.** One line each: where it is and the fix. Omit if none.
57	
58	**What's working.** One to three specific things to keep, and why.
59	```

**First read.** The eye goes first to the big serif headline, "Run the waiting list for your garden without the spreadsheet". It then goes across to the two green plots in the Elm Row map and down to the green "Add your garden" button. The page reads as a calm, plain product page for allotment or community gardens. The hero's two halves now fill the same width as the nav and the four cards, so the top of the page feels settled. On tablet and phone the map stacks under the button. On phone the section heading now wraps to two lines. Widescreen looks the same as desktop, centered in a wider margin.

**What it's for.** It tells a garden organizer that Plotwise runs their waiting list and offers each free plot to the next person in line, and it asks them to add their garden.

**Verdict.** The fixes made the hero line up and gave the section a heading that belongs to this product, so the page does its job a little better. The biggest thing still in the way is unchanged: the one picture on the page shows free and taken plots, not the offer of a free plot to the next person on the list, which is what the headline promises.

**Finding status**
- plot-map-wrong-idea: open. The map is the same at all four viewports: 12 plots, plots 3 and 8 marked "Free", and a Free/Taken key. Nothing shows a waiting list or an offer to the next person.
- plot-map-ragged-right-edge: closed. On desktop the card now ends at x 1216, level with "Sign in" and the fourth card (the plot map title box is now 528 px wide, up from 418). On widescreen it ends at x 1536, the same edge as the nav and the cards.
- examples-or-rules: open. "one reminder before rent is due in March" and "a week to say yes" are unchanged at all four viewports and still read as fixed rules. Only the maker can say which they are.
- generic-section-heading: closed. "From the waiting list to work days" is built from words already on the page and names the first card and the last card at all four viewports. It is still 22 px serif.

**New problems.**
- Phone: the new section heading wraps to two lines (29 characters on the first line), so "days" sits alone on the second line, under a heading that otherwise reads as one phrase.

**What would move it most**
1. The plot map shows the wrong idea (taste). The viewer sees which plots are free but not the step that only Plotwise does: it offers a free plot to the next person on the waiting list. So the hero picture supports "keeps the plots" and not the headline's promise. Source: Tufte, direct labels. Fix direction: show a free plot going to the next person in line, for example a short waiting list beside the map, with plot 3 marked as offered to the first person on it. Use only states and names that the product really has, and the maker must supply them. Do not invent sample growers. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

**Smaller things.**
- Rent reminders card and plot offers card: the March reminder and the week to say yes read as fixed product limits. The maker must say if they are examples or rules, then the copy must show which. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
- Section heading on phone: "days" sits alone on the second line. Keep "work days" together, for example with a non-breaking space between the two words, or let the heading set slightly tighter at this width. Viewports: phone.
- Plot map card on tablet: the card ends at about x 491, but the cards below run to x 736. This was the same before the fixes. Let the card run the full content width, or match a card column. Viewports: tablet.

**What's working.**
- The hero now holds two columns that end on the same right edge as the nav and the card row, so the top of the page reads as one grid on desktop and widescreen.
- Only the free plots, the button, and the key swatch use the single green, so the eye goes straight to the free plots and to the action.
- The new heading tells the viewer that the four cards follow a grower from the waiting list through to the work days, and it uses only words that the page already has.

1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:

The hero's two halves now fill the same width as the nav and the four cards, so the top of the page feels settled. On tablet and phone the map stacks under the button. On phone the section heading now wraps to two lines. Widescreen looks the same as desktop, centered in a wider margin.

4	
5	**Verdict.** The fixes made the hero line up and gave the section a heading that belongs to this product, so the page does its job a little better. The biggest thing still in the way is unchanged: the one picture on the page shows free and taken plots, not the offer of a free plot to the next person on the list, which is what the headline promises.

17	1. The plot map shows the wrong idea (taste). The viewer sees which plots are free but not the step that only Plotwise does: it offers a free plot to the next person on the waiting list. So the hero picture supports "keeps the plots" and not the headline's promise. Source: Tufte, direct labels. Fix direction: show a free plot going to the next person in line, for example a short waiting list beside the map, with plot 3 marked as offered to the first person on it. Use only states and names that the product really has, and the maker must supply them. Do not invent sample growers. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

content.content:
1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and no element the fix added or changed is a template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but an element the fix added or changed is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the fix added or changed as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. Added means the after image has it and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background. Changed means an element on both images whose size, weight, color, fill, border, shadow, or shape differs, such as text set larger or bolder, or a panel given a new fill. An added or changed element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and an element the fix added or changed is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33

summary:
**First read.** The eye lands on the big serif headline, "Run the waiting list for your garden without the spreadsheet". It then jumps to the two dark green plots, 3 and 8, in the Elm Row plot map. The page reads as a calm, plain tool for a community garden. The map says "here are the free plots", but it does not say "Plotwise offers them to the next person in line". On the phone the page stacks into one column, and "work days" now stays together on the second line of the section heading. On the tablet the plot map card now runs to the same right edge as the cards below it. Desktop and widescreen look the same as before.

**What it's for.** To get a garden organizer to click "Add your garden" by showing that Plotwise runs the waiting list and offers each free plot to the next grower in line.

**Verdict.** The two layout fixes worked, and the phone and tablet pages now hold together. The biggest problem is still the plot map. It shows free and taken plots but not the step that sells the product: a free plot going to the next person on the waiting list.

**Finding status**
- plot-map-wrong-idea: open. At all four viewports the map is unchanged: 12 plots, plots 3 and 8 marked Free, a Free/Taken key, the title "Elm Row Gardens: plots 3 and 8 are free", and no waiting list or offer in or beside it.
- examples-or-rules: open. At all four viewports the copy is word for word the same: "one reminder before rent is due in March" and "a week to say yes" still read as fixed rules. Only the maker can say which they are.
- heading-orphan-days-phone: closed. On the phone the h2 still takes 2 lines (measured), but it now breaks as "From the waiting list to / work days", so "days" is no longer alone.
- plot-map-card-width-tablet: closed. On the tablet the plot map card now spans x 32 to 736 (the title measures 662 px wide, from x 53), the same right edge as the cards below. The wider plots add no new element and are not a template tell.

**New problems.** None.

**What would move it most**
1. Plot map, hero (Elm Row card): the viewer sees which plots are free, but not the step only Plotwise does, which is offering a free plot to the next person on the waiting list. So the picture backs up "keeps the plots" and not the promise in the headline and subhead (Tufte, direct labels). Show a free plot going to the next person in line. For example, put a short waiting list beside or under the map, with plot 3 marked as offered to the first person on it. The maker must supply the real states and names; do not invent sample growers. Taste. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

**Smaller things.**
- Plot offers and Rent reminders card copy: the maker must say whether "March" and "a week" are examples or fixed rules, and the copy must then show which. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

**What's working.**
- The quiet palette uses one green, and only for the action and the free plots, so the button and plots 3 and 8 are the only things that pull the eye.
- The tablet layout now has one shared right edge from the hero card down through the cards, so the column reads as one block.
- The phone heading now breaks after "to", which keeps "work days" together as one phrase.

**First read.** The eye lands on the big serif headline, "Run the waiting list for your garden without the spreadsheet". It then jumps to the two dark green plots, 3 and 8, in the Elm Row plot map. The page reads as a calm, plain tool for a community garden. The map says "here are the free plots", but it does not say "Plotwise offers them to the next person in line". On the phone the page stacks into one column, and "work days" now stays together on the second line of the section heading. On the tablet the plot map card now runs to the same right edge as the cards below it. Desktop and widescreen look the same as before.

**What it's for.** To get a garden organizer to click "Add your garden" by showing that Plotwise runs the waiting list and offers each free plot to the next grower in line.

**Verdict.** The two layout fixes worked, and the phone and tablet pages now hold together. The biggest problem is still the plot map. It shows free and taken plots but not the step that sells the product: a free plot going to the next person on the waiting list.

**Finding status**
- plot-map-wrong-idea: open. At all four viewports the map is unchanged: 12 plots, plots 3 and 8 marked Free, a Free/Taken key, the title "Elm Row Gardens: plots 3 and 8 are free", and no waiting list or offer in or beside it.
- examples-or-rules: open. At all four viewports the copy is word for word the same: "one reminder before rent is due in March" and "a week to say yes" still read as fixed rules. Only the maker can say which they are.
- heading-orphan-days-phone: closed. On the phone the h2 still takes 2 lines (measured), but it now breaks as "From the waiting list to / work days", so "days" is no longer alone.
- plot-map-card-width-tablet: closed. On the tablet the plot map card now spans x 32 to 736 (the title measures 662 px wide, from x 53), the same right edge as the cards below. The wider plots add no new element and are not a template tell.

**New problems.** None.

**What would move it most**
1. Plot map, hero (Elm Row card): the viewer sees which plots are free, but not the step only Plotwise does, which is offering a free plot to the next person on the waiting list. So the picture backs up "keeps the plots" and not the promise in the headline and subhead (Tufte, direct labels). Show a free plot going to the next person in line. For example, put a short waiting list beside or under the map, with plot 3 marked as offered to the first person on it. The maker must supply the real states and names; do not invent sample growers. Taste. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

**Smaller things.**
- Plot offers and Rent reminders card copy: the maker must say whether "March" and "a week" are examples or fixed rules, and the copy must then show which. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

**What's working.**
- The quiet palette uses one green, and only for the action and the free plots, so the button and plots 3 and 8 are the only things that pull the eye.
- The tablet layout now has one shared right edge from the hero card down through the cards, so the column reads as one block.
- The phone heading now breaks after "to", which keeps "work days" together as one phrase.

I ran four rounds and stopped after round 4.

**Why I stopped.** Neither of the skill's two stop rules has fired yet. One ranked finding is still open, and round 4 closed two findings. But both findings that are left need content that only you have, so I can't change anything more in the page. Under the rules, I would have to run two more rounds on a page that doesn't change, just to record "nothing closed" twice. That only costs time and money, so I stopped now. Your content is the only thing that can move the page forward.

**What changed** (in `index.html` and `styles.css`):
- **Phone:** the page no longer scrolls sideways. The nav has its own row under the logo, and each link is 31 px tall. The plot map sits under the button, and the cards are in one column.
- **Tablet:** the cards are in two columns, the plot tiles are all one width, and the map card runs to the same right edge as the cards.
- **Wide screens:** the content is capped at 1152 px and centered. The hero uses the same four columns as the cards, so the plot map lines up with them.
- **Card text:** the titles are in weight 500 and the darker text color, with a small gap below them. Before, they looked the same as the body text. The section heading is in the serif at 22 px, the same size as the logo.
- **Plot map:** plots 3 and 8 now say "Free" on the tile. The title now reads "Elm Row Gardens: plots 3 and 8 are free".
- **Copy:** I made only two small edits. The section heading changed from "What Plotwise does" to "From the waiting list to work days", using words already on the page. The card text no longer leaves one word alone on its last line.

**Last first read and verdict (round 4).** The eye goes to the serif headline, then to the two green free plots, then to the button. The page reads as a calm, plain tool for a community garden. The critic said the layout fixes worked and the page holds together at all four screen sizes. The biggest problem is still the plot map.

**Still open, because they need your content:**
1. **The plot map (ranked #1, all screen sizes).** It shows which plots are free and which are taken. It doesn't show what the headline promises: a free plot offered to the next person on the waiting list. The fix is a short waiting list beside or under the map, with plot 3 marked as offered to the first person. For that I need the real states the product uses (for example "offered" and "accepted") and the names or labels it shows. I didn't make up sample growers.
2. **The "Plot offers" and "Rent reminders" cards (all screen sizes).** "Rent is due in March" and "a week to say yes" read as fixed limits of the product. You need to say whether they are examples or rules, and then the copy can show which.

Nothing is worse than before, and the rechecks found no template tells in the changes. I haven't committed the changes.

The loop folder is `.crit-loop/` inside the project folder, because I couldn't write outside the project. It isn't in `.gitignore`, so delete it or ignore it before you commit.
